section_summary: This section covers diplomatic, political, and economic developments in Japan between July and November 1938 during the expanding Sino-Japanese conflict. Major diplomatic topics include disputes with the United States and Great Britain over property damages and rights in China, border hostilities with the Soviet Union at Changkufeng, and the cabinet crisis culminating in Foreign Minister Kazushige Ugaki's resignation over the establishment of the China Board (Tai Shi In). Prime Minister Fumimaro Konoe briefly held the foreign portfolio before appointing Hachiro Arita, as Japan signaled its rejection of the Nine-Power Treaty framework and asserted paramountcy in East Asia. Domestically, the section documents Japan's intensifying mobilization of materials, foreign trade restrictions, capital rationing, and economic reorganization under the National General Mobilization Law, evolving toward an indigenous form of totalitarianism centered on the Emperor.

subfiles.about: The concluding pages of Ambassador Grew's report on his July 4, 1938 interview with Foreign Minister Ugaki regarding American property damages and extraterritoriality in China.
subfiles.summary: Ugaki urges local settlement of China property damage, insisting operational necessity justifies action regardless of nationality, citing Chinese use of American church property in several provinces, and listing disrespectful American periodicals.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3081: Report of Interview with Japanese Foreign Minister Ugaki (concluding section)

subfiles.about: A personal letter from Stanley K. Hornbeck commending Ambassador Grew on the completeness and substance of Despatch No. 3081.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck praises Grew's Despatch 3081 on the Ugaki conversation as thorough, bringing it to Hull's and Welles's attention.
subfiles.title: Letter from Stanley K. Hornbeck to Joseph C. Grew regarding Despatch No. 3081

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew alerts Hornbeck to examine personally the Embassy's July 8 despatch reporting his interview with Foreign Minister Ugaki.
subfiles.summary: Grew suggests Hornbeck and Hull personally examine his July 8 despatch detailing his July 4 conference with Foreign Minister Ugaki.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 486 from Tokyo regarding Despatch of July 8

subfiles.about: A State Department memorandum noting that Tokyo Despatch No. 3097 transmits Foreign Minister Ugaki's comments on the protection of American lives and property.
subfiles.summary: Schuler notes Despatch 3097 translates Ugaki's July 4 remarks to Grew, already fully covered in the earlier Despatch 3081.
subfiles.title: State Department Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 3097

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew transmits an official translation of Foreign Minister Ugaki's statement on American property in China along with his own diplomatic rejoinder.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew transmits the translated text of Foreign Minister Ugaki's comments from their July 4 interview regarding the protection of American lives and property in China. Ugaki maintained that Japanese attacks on American properties were an unavoidable military necessity when Chinese forces established positions nearby or occupied church compounds, citing incidents in Shunteh, Fenyang, Chunyin, and Tsingtao. Ugaki argued that the United States should seek to prevent Chinese military utilization of American properties rather than placing sole responsibility on Japan. In response, Grew reiterated that damaged American properties were largely separated from Chinese military objectives and reaffirmed that the U.S. holds Japan responsible for all such losses.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3097: Protection of Lives and Property of American Nationals

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for a memorandum recording a conversation with Count Kabayama of the Japanese House of Peers regarding the Sino-Japanese conflict.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Ballantine's memo on a conversation with Count Kabayama examining the Sino-Japanese conflict through Japanese history and temperament.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet for Memorandum on Conversation with Count Kabayama

subfiles.about: A military intelligence report reviewing Japanese domestic political reforms, economic measures, and foreign relations during July 1938.
subfiles.summary: The Tokyo Military Attaché details domestic political and economic developments, including proposed reforms of the House of Peers and Diet electoral system, difficulties in enforcing a ten percent budget reduction, the cancellation of the 1940 Tokyo Olympic Games, and the establishment of a 300-million-yen gold revolving fund for export industries. In foreign affairs, the report discusses Prime Minister Konoe's declaration refusing any further dealings with Chiang Kai-shek, diplomatic frictions with Britain and France over China and the Paracel Islands, Manuel Quezon's visit to Tokyo, and press interviews with Soviet defector General Liushkov. The report highlights severe military tensions along the Manchukuo-Soviet border near Changkufeng, noting high-level Japanese imperial conferences and the risk of war with the Soviet Union.
subfiles.title: Military Intelligence Report No. 9486: Comment on Current Events (Japan - Political)

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for Telegram No. 572 reporting delays in Anglo-Japanese discussions and Ugaki's weakening political position.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Tokyo telegram on postponed Ugaki-Craigie talks, Craigie planning to warn Japan, attributed to Ugaki's weakened standing and military fears.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet for Telegram No. 572 regarding Postponement of Ugaki-Craigie Meetings

subfiles.about: A consular report transmitting Japanese press translations on munitions industry labor shortages, factory expansion, and university funding in the Nagoya district.
subfiles.summary: American Vice Consul Charles H. Stephan transmits translations of three articles from Nagoya newspapers illustrating regional economic adjustments under wartime conditions. The first article details a acute labor shortage in Aichi Prefecture where public works and river improvement projects were stalled because laborers were absorbed by the booming munitions industry. The second reports a major expansion of electric power capacity at the Mitsubishi Heavy Industries airplane motor factory to 10,000 kilowatts. The third reports the Ministry of Education's decision to more than double the funding for Nagoya University to establish science, engineering, and medical colleges aimed at supporting continental expansion.
subfiles.title: Consular Report: News Items from Nagoya

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports the sudden resignation of Foreign Minister Ugaki following cabinet disagreements over the control of the projected China board.
subfiles.summary: Grew confidentially confirms Foreign Minister Ugaki resigned amid a cabinet clash over whether the proposed China board would be under Foreign Office jurisdiction, possibly to force an Imperial decision in the civilian-military dispute.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 635: Resignation of Foreign Minister Ugaki

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports the acceptance of Ugaki's resignation, Prime Minister Konoe's assumption of the foreign portfolio, and the surrounding political context.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports Ugaki's resignation accepted, Konoe assuming Foreign/Overseas Affairs; Ugaki had refused the Army's unconstitutional autonomous China organ demand, press blamed him for disunity, reflecting enduring division over China policy.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 636: Acceptance of Ugaki's Resignation and Appointment of Konoe

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for a despatch from Riga enclosing newspaper interviews with Japanese Generals Ugaki and Araki.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Riga despatch transmitting a Segodnya interview with Generals Ugaki and Araki on Japanese political affairs.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet for Despatch No. 1391 from Riga

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for Telegram No. 589 regarding ultra-nationalist press agitation against Foreign Minister Ugaki over diplomatic appointments.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Tokyo telegram on ultra-nationalist press attacks on Ugaki over delayed Anti-Comintern-related appointments, expected to subside once announced.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet for Telegram No. 589 regarding Press Attacks on Ugaki

subfiles.about: A State Department analytical memorandum evaluating Tokyo Embassy despatches on the newly established China Board and Foreign Minister Ugaki's resignation.
subfiles.summary: Schuler analyzes Despatches 3300/3320 on the new China Board under the Premier and four ministers, seeing it as Konoe's bid to keep control from the military; Ugaki's resignation failed to shift public opinion toward civilian control, as field commanders will continue dominating China policy.
subfiles.title: State Department Memorandum on the China Board and Ugaki's Resignation

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew provides a comprehensive assessment of the circumstances, public reception, and diplomatic fallout of Foreign Minister Ugaki's resignation.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports Ugaki's September 29 resignation after lone opposition to the China Board, fearing it would gut the Foreign Office; press and public backed centralized control, with Sato/Arita also resigning and Saito, Shiratori, Matsuoka, Shigemitsu speculated as successors.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3320: Resignation of Foreign Minister Ugaki

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew analyzes the formation, institutional framework, and political significance of the China Board (Tai Shi In).
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew examines the impending establishment of the China Board (Tai Shi In), viewing it as part of a sustained drift away from party cabinets toward centralized policy organs like Imperial Headquarters and the five-minister conference. Operating directly under the Premier with four vice directors (War, Navy, Foreign, and Finance/Commerce Ministers), the Board is structured into general affairs, economics, and cultural relations bureaus, with field branches planned for Peiping, Kalgan, and Shanghai. Grew interprets the organ as Prime Minister Konoe's endeavor to prevent exclusive military control over China policy, but warns that establishing an overarching body for Chinese affairs risks permanently subordinating civilian diplomacy and concentrating power.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3300: The China Board (Tai Shi In)

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports the official appointments of Hachiro Arita as Foreign Minister and Yoshiaki Hatta as Minister for Overseas Affairs.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports Arita appointed Foreign Minister, relieving Konoe, and Hatta, former South Manchuria Railway vice president, as Overseas Affairs Minister.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 691: Cabinet Appointments of Hachiro Arita and Yoshiaki Hatta

subfiles.about: A State Department assessment of Hachiro Arita's unexpected selection as Japanese Minister for Foreign Affairs.
subfiles.summary: Schuler welcomes Arita's surprise Foreign Minister appointment as preferable to extremists like Matsuoka, but warns the military's acceptance may be mere diplomatic window dressing.
subfiles.title: State Department Memorandum on the Appointment of Hachiro Arita as Foreign Minister

subfiles.about: Schuler highlights key points from Despatch No. 3392 regarding Arita's outlook and Embassy discussions with the Japanese Foreign Office.
subfiles.summary: Schuler notes Despatch 3392: Arita shares liberals' 'no road back' China view; Dooman learned from Yoshizawa that even the military sees American/British capital as needed for China, though no settlement is possible without U.S. recognition of the 'new situation.'
subfiles.title: State Department Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 3392

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew analyzes Hachiro Arita's appointment as Foreign Minister, Embassy discussions on American rights, and Japan's forthcoming New Order declaration.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew evaluates the appointment of Hachiro Arita as Minister for Foreign Affairs, concluding that while Arita is personally honorable, his acceptance of the post signifies agreement with the five-minister China Organ and Japan's immutable continental objectives. The despatch recounts Embassy Counselor Dooman's meeting with American Bureau Director Yoshizawa, where Dooman cautioned that Japan was heading toward Tokugawa-style seclusion and that U.S. loans were impossible while equal opportunity was denied. Yoshizawa countered that American recognition of the 'new situation' was essential, leading Grew to anticipate that following the capture of Hankow, Japan's imminent official declaration will repudiate the Nine-Power Treaty and assert paramountcy over East Asia.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3392: Appointment of Mr. Hachiro Arita as Minister for Foreign Affairs

subfiles.about: Schuler reviews and evaluates Max W. Schmidt's comprehensive Embassy study on Japanese national mobilization.
subfiles.summary: Schuler summarizes Despatch 3380 and Schmidt's study tracing Japan's mobilization law from 1918 to 1938, linking it to totalitarian ambitions, but cautions Japan lacks European totalitarian prerequisites and may revert to its oligarchical system postwar.
subfiles.title: State Department Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 3380 regarding National Mobilization

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew transmits an exhaustive Embassy research memorandum by Max W. Schmidt detailing the evolution and apparatus of national mobilization in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew forwards an extensive research monograph prepared by Third Secretary Max W. Schmidt tracing the development of Japan's state mobilization. In his covering despatch, Grew characterizes Japan's political trajectory not as standard European fascism under a dictator, but as a unique 'totalitarianism sui generis' that integrates national life around the Emperor cult. Schmidt's memorandum details the legislative history from World War I-era munitions laws through the 1927 Bureau of Resources, the 1935 Cabinet Deliberative Body, the 1937 Cabinet Planning Board, and the sweeping National General Mobilization Law of 1938. The study documents extensive wartime control mechanisms, including state regulation of foreign exchange, the textile link system, strict import-export prohibitions under Law No. 92 and Law No. 65, industrial capital rationing, and materials allocation across all major manufacturing sectors.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3380: National Mobilization (enclosing memorandum 'Mobilization in Japan')
